chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Carl George and learning that players practice licks
summary: Carl George proposes trading licks; Maxwell learns great players work up solos.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And it seemed like at that time, '39 and the '40s, everybody's pretty excited about jazz. They all liked to talk about it, Teddy Wilson had just started up his band and he had a trumpet player named Carl George.
Yeah, I remember, excellent trumpet player.
Yeah. And he and I kind of got friendly and he said something funny to me, it struck me as funny, he said, you know, you and I are buddies, we ought to trade licks. And I said, what do you mean?

I'd never heard of this. He knew a lot of licks, you know. When he would play he would take the licks he'd put together, and he did it great. I really love the way he plays, I thought he was a good player. But he had these things that he'd practice and these things are all eye-openers to me. See, I thought that musicians like -- God gave you a gift, you know, you took a drink of whiskey and you either had it or you didn't. You practiced your instrument, got technique, practiced scales and chromatics. When you went to play you would be inspired and everything would come out. And it's been a long, long learning

process, and it's going on even today for me, that this isn't true, that guys -- they practice things, they practice fragments, they practice other people's solos or their own solos, and they're not ashamed to admit -- you know, good players, even like Ben Webster. He would work up solos, he would work up two or three solos.
